Greatness PhaaS Adds Device Code Phishing to Bypass MFA and Steal Tokens

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 15 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) toolkit known as Greatness has become the latest crimeware solution to add support for device code phishing, a rapidly growing cyber threat that abuses the legitimate OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant to bypass Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and seize control of user accounts. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RingCentral voicemail phishing lure delivered despite SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure (safe-sender bypass) · [LLM] Navigation / DNS to Greatness PhaaS phishing infrastructure domains · [LLM] Inbound email containing Microsoft device-code / devicelogin URL from external phishing context · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New device registration / PRT generation minutes after a device-code sign-in
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] M365 authentication from known Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Entra ID device-code flow authentication (Greatness device-code phishing redemption) · [LLM] Malicious inbox rule created hours after anomalous M365 sign-in · [LLM] Post-compromise Microsoft Graph enumeration across many M365 resources in minutes · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Entra ID device-code flow authentication (Greatness device-code phishing redemption) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful Entra sign-ins completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant, the specific MFA-bypass primitive Greatness added. Device-code flows are rare and legitimately user-initiated, so a successful device-code sign-in from an unexpected IP/UA is high-signal for an attacker redeeming a phished code. Rationale: Keys on the article's central primitive — the OAuth device authorization grant added to Greatness — via the AuthenticationProcessingDetails "Device Code" marker (canonical Entra sign-in signal for this flow). Covers reviewer suggestions #1/#3 (anomalous device-code initiation + MFA bypass). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code onboarding of shared/kiosk devices, IoT, or conference-room hardware
  • Developers using `az login --use-device-code` or PowerShell/CLI device-code auth
  • Smart-TV / streaming-app style sign-ins to Microsoft 365 apps
  • Break-glass admin using device-code on an unmanaged host
  • Users completing MFA registration on a secondary device
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" and AppDisplayName in ("Microsoft Azure CLI", "Microsoft Azure PowerShell", "Microsoft Authentication Broker"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the IP/UserAgent/geo matches the user's normal pattern and whether a corresponding help-desk or CLI/device onboarding exists; check if the same UPN had an inbound phish with a 'short code' lure in the prior hour. 2) Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), require re-auth, and reset credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot to any device registered by that UPN in the following minutes, new inbox rules, and Graph enumeration of Outlook/Teams/SharePoint (see related UCs) — token validity can persist for weeks.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, DeviceTrustType, IsInteractive
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IsInteractive, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

M365 authentication from known Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any Entra sign-in or endpoint connection involving the ZeroBEC-observed Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214, which was seen replaying stolen tokens against a victim tenant for over two weeks post-phish. A named IOC makes this alerting-grade. Rationale: Uses the single hard IOC ZeroBEC published (38.248.95.214) confirmed as an active AiTM proxy re-authenticating against a victim tenant weeks after the phish — very low FP as a fixed malicious IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP later reassigned to a benign hoster and reused by a legitimate proxy/VPN
  • Security-team sandbox detonation of the phishing chain from a lab egress that shares the ASN
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation traffic from your own tooling
  • Shared NAT if the malicious host is behind a large provider (rare for /32)
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every UPN authenticated from 38.248.95.214 and the resources/apps accessed; treat each as a candidate token-replay victim. 2) Contain: revoke sign-in sessions and refresh tokens for all matched users, force password reset, and block the IP at the identity provider (named location) and perimeter. 3) Hunt: for each victim, review device registrations, inbox-rule creation, and Graph resource enumeration in the following hours; token lifetime means access may continue absent revocation.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, Application, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ErrorCode, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ResultType, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New device registration / PRT generation minutes after a device-code sign-in AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a successful device-code Entra sign-in with an Entra device registration by the same user within 60 minutes — the persistence step Microsoft observed where the actor registers a device to mint a Primary Refresh Token for long-term access. Article-specific temporal chain, not a generic device-join alert. Rationale: Directly encodes Microsoft's reported post-compromise behaviour (register a device within minutes to generate a PRT) chained to the device-code sign-in — the temporal join is what makes it TP-specific rather than routine device enrollment. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new-hire or device-refresh enrollment where the user genuinely used device-code onboarding
  • Autopilot / Intune bulk provisioning windows
  • User enrolling a personal BYOD device after a normal sign-in
  • Help-desk assisted device registration during ticket resolution
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the registered device's OS/name/trust-type and whether it matches corporate managed hardware; verify the sign-in IP against the user's baseline. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable/delete the newly registered device object, revoke the user's tokens (invalidates the PRT), and force credential reset. 3) Hunt: check for inbox-rule creation and Graph enumeration from the same session, and search other users showing device-code sign-in followed by device registration.
let deviceCodeSignins = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"

| project SigninTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SigninIP = IPAddress, AppDisplayName;

| project RegTime = TimeGenerated, SigninTime, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, SigninTime), UserPrincipalName = TargetUpn, OperationName, SigninIP, AppDisplayName, InitiatedBy
| order by RegTime desc

Malicious inbox rule created hours after anomalous M365 sign-in AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates an anomalous or device-code Entra sign-in with an Exchange inbox-rule (New/Set-InboxRule) that deletes, moves, or forwards mail, created within 24 hours — the delayed defense-evasion step ZeroBEC/Microsoft observed attackers use to hide traffic and stage exfiltration. Ties two log sources rather than firing on rule creation alone. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific 'wait several hours before setting up malicious inbox rules' tradecraft by joining the rule creation to the preceding device-code/risky sign-in, and filters to hide/forward/delete actions that indicate evasion or BEC staging. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/003/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately creating a forward-to-manager or vacation redirect rule after a normal sign-in
  • Mailbox migration tooling recreating rules
  • Admin-provisioned org-wide transport/inbox rules
  • Power-user building folder-sort rules that move mail to subfolders
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "ForwardTo" and ClientIP in (SigninIP)) or Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage", "Junk")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the exact rule Parameters — external ForwardTo/RedirectTo or delete-on-receipt to 'RSS/Deleted Items' are near-certain malicious; confirm the preceding sign-in was device-code/risky. 2) Contain: remove the inbox rule, revoke user sessions, reset credentials, and add the forwarding target to blocklists. 3) Hunt: enumerate all mailboxes for similar rules created since the campaign start, and review sent-items/Graph pulls for data already exfiltrated.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| where RawEventData has_any ("ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "Junk", "Deleted Items")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let anomSignins = SigninLogs

| where ResultType == 0

OfficeActivity

| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| where Parameters has_any ("ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "Junk", "DeletedItems")

| where TimeGenerated between (SigninTime .. SigninTime + 24h)
| project RuleTime = TimeGenerated, SigninTime, HoursDelay = datetime_diff('hour', TimeGenerated, SigninTime), UserId, Operation, ClientIP, SigninIP, Parameters
| order by RuleTime desc

RingCentral voicemail phishing lure delivered despite SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure (safe-sender bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound voicemail-themed emails impersonating RingCentral that FAILED SPF/DKIM/DMARC yet were Delivered to the inbox — the exact safe-sender-exclusion abuse ZeroBEC documented for Greatness RingCentral campaigns against actual RingCentral customers. Article-specific because the fidelity comes from delivered-despite-auth-failure, not the impersonation alone. Rationale: Combines the article's lure (RingCentral voicemail) with its detection-grade twist — delivered to inbox despite SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure via safe-sender exclusion — which is what distinguishes this from ordinary brand-impersonation phishing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine RingCentral voicemail notifications from a misconfigured connector that fails DMARC
  • Legitimate third-party voicemail-to-email services on the tenant safe-sender list
  • Internal test/phishing-simulation campaigns using RingCentral themes
  • Newsletter/marketing mail from RingCentral that trips DKIM alignment
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain endswith "ringcentral.com" and AuthenticationDetails has "pass")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open EmailUrlInfo for the message, extract the embedded URL and check it against the Greatness .cfd/.one IOC domains; confirm the sender is not a sanctioned RingCentral connector. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide (same cluster), and if any recipient clicked, treat as device-code/AiTM candidate. 3) Hunt: audit and tighten the RingCentral-domain safe-sender/allow-list exclusions (per ZeroBEC guidance), and review UrlClickEvents for click-throughs.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox"
| where SenderFromDomain has "ringcentral" or SenderDisplayName has "RingCentral" or Subject has_any ("voicemail", "voice message", "new voice")
| where AuthenticationDetails has "fail"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

EmailEvents

| where SenderFromDomain has "ringcentral" or SenderDisplayName has "RingCentral" or Subject has_any ("voicemail", "voice message", "new voice")
| where AuthenticationDetails has "fail"
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Navigation / DNS to Greatness PhaaS phishing infrastructure domains AIDelivery High
Alerts on any email URL, DNS resolution, or endpoint connection to the ZeroBEC-listed Greatness operator domains (hashmashryshl.cfd, hashmashryly.cfd, onlineyoutlook.one, willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd, lookatcreatilcense.one, wbajp.feelingfor.com). Named IOC domains make this alerting-grade infrastructure coverage. Rationale: Ships the pre-extracted Greatness IOC domains across DNS/web/network so any resolution or click is caught regardless of the delivery channel; fixed adversary domains give low FP and cover reviewer suggestion #4 (Greatness infrastructure indicators). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-team sandbox/URL-detonation of the phishing chain from a managed host
  • Threat-intel crawler or proxy pre-fetch of the IOC domains
  • Passive-DNS/monitoring tooling resolving IOCs for enrichment
  • Domain re-registration and repurpose after takedown (stale IOC)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved or navigated to the domain and whether it followed an inbound RingCentral/voicemail lure; check for a subsequent device-code sign-in. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domains at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a full click-through occurred, and revoke the user's tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep EmailUrlInfo/UrlClickEvents tenant-wide for the same domains and pivot on the resolving IP for sibling infrastructure.
let iocDomains = dynamic(["hashmashryshl.cfd","hashmashryly.cfd","onlineyoutlook.one","willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd","lookatcreatilcense.one","wbajp.feelingfor.com","addtorimez.gba","pleasebeatwithlllocliad.gbs"]);
union
( DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any (iocDomains) | project Timestamp, Source="Network", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator=RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName ),
( DeviceEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any (iocDomains) | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceEvent", DeviceName, AccountName, Indicator=RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName )
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocDomains = dynamic(["hashmashryshl.cfd","hashmashryly.cfd","onlineyoutlook.one","willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd","lookatcreatilcense.one","wbajp.feelingfor.com","addtorimez.gba","pleasebeatwithlllocliad.gbs"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (iocDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Kind="DNS" ),
( ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (iocDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=Url, Kind="Web" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-compromise Microsoft Graph enumeration across many M365 resources in minutes AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single principal accessing an unusually broad set of Microsoft 365 resources (Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Exchange, OneDrive) within a short window after token replay — the ZeroBEC-observed post-auth Graph enumeration that follows a Greatness device-code/AiTM compromise. Fan-out on distinct resources, not a single access. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific post-compromise action — replayed tokens enumerating Outlook/Teams/SharePoint/Exchange/OneDrive via Graph — as a per-user resource fan-out within a tight window, which surfaces rapid discovery without alerting on any single normal resource access. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1526/
ATT&CKT1526 T1087.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users / executives genuinely opening many M365 apps at start of day
  • SSO into a suite launcher that pre-authenticates several resources at once
  • Migration or backup service accounts touching many workloads (exclude with the machine-account filter)
  • Mobile devices refreshing tokens for multiple apps after a network change
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountUpn has_any ("svc-", "backup", "sync"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the fan-out originated from a device-code/AiTM sign-in or the Greatness proxy IP, and whether the IP/UA is anomalous for the user. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and reset credentials for the principal; block the source IP if attacker-controlled. 3) Hunt: review what was actually read (mailbox, SharePoint/OneDrive downloads) and correlate with subsequent inbox-rule creation or device registration.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize ResourceCount = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ResourceCount >= 5   // 5+ distinct M365 resources touched by one user in 10m = enumeration fan-out (baseline P95 ~= 3)
| where Resources has_any ("Office 365 Exchange Online", "Microsoft Teams", "Office 365 SharePoint Online", "Microsoft Graph", "OneDrive")
| order by ResourceCount desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| summarize ResourceCount = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where ResourceCount >= 5   // 5+ distinct resources in 10m indicates Graph enumeration fan-out
| where Resources has_any ("Office 365 Exchange Online", "Microsoft Teams", "Office 365 SharePoint Online", "Microsoft Graph", "OneDrive")
| order by ResourceCount desc

Inbound email containing Microsoft device-code / devicelogin URL from external phishing context AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails whose embedded URL points to a Microsoft device-login endpoint (microsoft.com/devicelogin, aka.ms/devicelogin, oauth2 devicecode) — the lure pattern Greatness/Okta describe where the victim is sent to the REAL Microsoft page to enter an attacker-generated short code. Article-specific: the page is legitimate, so the signal is a devicelogin link arriving via external mail. Rationale: Targets the specific device-code phishing lure vector (a link to the genuine Microsoft devicelogin/devicecode endpoint arriving via inbound mail), which the article/Okta call out as the 'short code + plausible reason' trick — covers reviewer suggestion #5. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1621
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT onboarding emails instructing users to complete device-code enrollment
  • Vendor/SaaS docs linking to aka.ms/devicelogin for CLI setup
  • Internal help-desk instructions for smart-device sign-in
  • Security-awareness training emails referencing device-code phishing
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "microsoft.com" and SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourorg.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the sender is external/unexpected and whether the body pressures the user to enter a code 'to listen to a voicemail / view a document'; correlate with UrlClickEvents. 2) Contain: quarantine matching messages tenant-wide; if a recipient clicked and a device-code sign-in followed, revoke tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to any successful device-code Entra sign-in for the recipients within the following hour and to the Greatness IOC domains in the same message.
let devUrls = dynamic(["microsoft.com/devicelogin","aka.ms/devicelogin","oauth2/v2.0/devicecode","oauth2/deviceauth"]);
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any (devUrls)
| join kind=inner ( EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered" | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url
| order by Timestamp desc

let devUrls = dynamic(["microsoft.com/devicelogin","aka.ms/devicelogin","oauth2/v2.0/devicecode","oauth2/deviceauth"]);
EmailUrlInfo
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any (devUrls)
| join kind=inner ( EmailEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered" | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Flowise additionalConfig database-path override in vector-upsert API request (CVE-2026-69259) · [LLM] Flowise node runtime spawns shell interpreter (post-exploit command execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Flowise node process writes SQLite DB file to system directory (arbitrary-write RCE primitive) · [LLM] Flowise node process writes to cron / systemd / SSH persistence path · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-69259: Flowise RCE via SQLite Record Manager Node
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Flowise additionalConfig database-path override in vector-upsert API request (CVE-2026-69259) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POSTs to Flowise ingestion endpoints carrying an `additionalConfig` payload that overrides the SQLite `database` path (or supplies TypeORM `entities`/`migrations` for JS-load RCE). This is the exact exploitation primitive for CVE-2026-69259 in FlowiseAI 3.1.2. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable input name `additionalConfig` reaching the Record Manager node via Flowise's `/api/v1/vector/upsert` and document-store ingestion endpoints, correlated with an out-of-tree path (`/etc/`, `/root/`, `.sqlite`) or TypeORM `entities`/`migrations` keys — the confirmed RCE vector. Body inspection requires the proxy/WAF to log request bodies. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/ • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate automation that passes overrideConfig/additionalConfig with a benign in-tree .flowise database path
  • Security scanners / internal pentest hitting the upsert endpoint
  • Developers testing custom Record Manager configs against a staging instance
  • Load-testing tools replaying recorded upsert requests
Suppression filter
| where not (Message has ".flowise" and Message !has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/cron", "/dev/shm", "entities", "migrations"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body for matched events; confirm whether `additionalConfig.database` (or TypeORM `entities`/`migrations`) points outside the `~/.flowise` directory to a system path. Identify the authenticated Flowise user/API key used. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, revoke the Flowise API key, and confirm the Flowise version — upgrade 3.1.2 → 3.1.3+ immediately. 3) Hunt: on the Flowise host pivot to node file-writes and child-process spawns in the following minutes (see companion UCs) to determine if the write/RCE succeeded.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/v1/vector/upsert", "/api/v1/prediction", "/api/v1/document-store")
| where Message has "additionalConfig" or RequestURL has "additionalConfig" or RequestContext has "additionalConfig"
| where Message has_any ("database", "/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/cron", "entities", "migrations", ".sqlite") or RequestURL has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", ".sqlite")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url IN ("*/api/v1/vector/upsert*","*/api/v1/prediction*","*/api/v1/document-store*","*additionalConfig*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_user_agent Web.url Web.uri_path Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where like(url,"%additionalConfig%") OR like(url,"%/api/v1/vector/upsert%") OR like(url,"%/api/v1/document-store%")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url IN ("*/api/v1/vector/upsert*","*/api/v1/prediction*","*/api/v1/document-store*","*additionalConfig*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_user_agent Web.url Web.uri_path Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where like(url,"%additionalConfig%") OR like(url,"%/api/v1/vector/upsert%") OR like(url,"%/api/v1/document-store%")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Flowise node process writes SQLite DB file to system directory (arbitrary-write RCE primitive) AIInstallation High
Detects the Flowise node runtime creating a .sqlite/.sqlite3/.db file outside its `.flowise` home in a sensitive system directory — the direct file-write artifact of the CVE-2026-69259 additionalConfig database-path override, which runs as root in the flowiseai/flowise:3.1.2 Docker image. Rationale: Directly grounded in the article's statement that the flaw lets an attacker 'write an SQLite database to an arbitrary filepath, which includes system directories' while the 3.1.2 Docker image 'runs as root'. Keys on node as the writer + SQLite extension + system path, explicitly excluding the legitimate `.flowise` home. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise misconfigured with DATABASE_PATH pointed at a non-default but legitimate directory (e.g. /var/lib/flowise)
  • Backup jobs copying database.sqlite into /root or /var for archival
  • Container image that bind-mounts the SQLite DB to a host system path by design
  • Admin manually relocating the Flowise DB during maintenance
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "/var/lib/flowise" and FolderPath !startswith "/opt/flowise"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath is a genuine system dir (not an approved custom DATABASE_PATH) and capture the file — a SQLite header ('SQLite format 3') in /etc or /root is exploitation. Note InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the writing UID (expect root). 2) Contain: isolate the container/host, snapshot the file for forensics, then delete the planted DB and upgrade Flowise to 3.1.3+. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the preceding upsert API request (web UC) and forward to any cron/persistence file writes or node-spawned shells to scope full RCE.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "nodejs", "node.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".sqlite" or FileName endswith ".sqlite3" or FileName endswith ".db"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/", "/usr/local/sbin/", "/usr/local/bin/", "/dev/shm/")
| where FolderPath !contains ".flowise"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".sqlite" or TargetFileName endswith ".sqlite3" or TargetFileName endswith ".db"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/var/spool/", "/usr/local/sbin/", "/usr/local/bin/", "/dev/shm/")
| where TargetFilePath !has ".flowise"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Flowise node process writes SQLite database to system directory
id: 6a1f2c84-3b7d-4e21-9a0c-5f2b1d9e7c44
description: node runtime creating a .sqlite/.db file outside .flowise in a sensitive system path - CVE-2026-69259 arbitrary-write primitive
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3hf-7cj6-3r4m
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '/nodejs'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.sqlite'
      - '.sqlite3'
      - '.db'
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/etc/'
      - '/root/'
      - '/var/spool/'
      - '/usr/local/sbin/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
  filter_home:
    TargetFilename|contains: '.flowise'
  condition: selection and not filter_home
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\/node(js)?$/i
| regex("^/(etc|root|var/spool|usr/local/(s?bin)|dev/shm)/", field=TargetFileName)
| TargetFileName=/\.(sqlite3?|db)$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/\.flowise/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Flowise node process writes to cron / systemd / SSH persistence path AIInstallation High
Detects the Flowise node runtime creating or modifying a file in cron, systemd, init, or SSH authorized_keys directories — the likely means of converting the CVE-2026-69259 root arbitrary-write into code execution and persistence. Rationale: The article states the write targets 'system directories' as root; the canonical way to weaponize a root arbitrary-write into RCE/persistence is dropping a crontab/systemd unit or root authorized_keys. A node process — which should only ever touch its `.flowise` dir — writing to any of these paths is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.002 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Flowise container entrypoint script legitimately templating a systemd unit or cron entry at startup (rare)
  • Configuration-management agent (Ansible/Chef) mislabeled as node writing cron files
  • Admin editing root crontab while a node debug session holds the shell
  • Backup tooling restoring /root/.ssh from a snapshot
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the written file — a cron line, systemd ExecStart, or new SSH key added by node is a confirmed persistence implant; capture the payload command/key. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the malicious cron/unit/key, kill the Flowise container, and rotate any credentials on the box; upgrade to 3.1.3+. 3) Hunt: enumerate all cron.d/systemd/init.d/authorized_keys entries created since the first suspicious upsert request, and check for outbound connections from the payload (node-spawned shell UC).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "nodejs")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/", "/etc/cron.daily/", "/etc/cron.hourly/", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron/", "/etc/systemd/system/", "/etc/init.d/", "/root/.ssh/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/", "/etc/cron.daily/", "/etc/cron.hourly/", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron/", "/etc/systemd/system/", "/etc/init.d/", "/root/.ssh/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise node runtime spawns shell interpreter (post-exploit command execution) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the Flowise node process spawning bash/sh/dash/zsh (or cmd/powershell) — behaviour Flowise never exhibits in normal operation, indicating command execution following CVE-2026-69259 exploitation (e.g. via a TypeORM entities JS payload loaded through additionalConfig). Rationale: The advisory is titled an RCE; a normal Flowise node server does not fork interactive shells, so node -> bash/sh/powershell (especially with -c, /dev/tcp, curl/wget/nc, or base64 tokens) is a strong post-exploitation indicator. Parent-child pairing (node parent) plus suspicious-arg tokens keeps fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Flowise Tool/Custom-Function node that legitimately shells out (e.g. an admin-authored code-interpreter tool)
  • Container healthcheck or entrypoint wrapper invoking sh -c at startup
  • npm lifecycle scripts running sh during in-container package install/upgrade
  • Monitoring agents embedded in the image spawning sh for metric collection
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "npm" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "ci", "run"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — reverse-shell (/dev/tcp, nc -e), downloader (curl|wget), or base64 blob confirms exploitation; benign `sh -c` from a known custom tool node may be expected. Identify the initiating node PID and its network peers. 2) Contain: kill the child process, isolate the container/host, block any outbound C2 IP, and revoke Flowise API keys; patch to 3.1.3+. 3) Hunt: correlate with preceding upsert API requests and node file-writes (companion UCs), and sweep other Flowise hosts for the same node->shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "nodejs")
| where FileName in~ ("bash", "sh", "dash", "zsh", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c", "/dev/tcp/", "curl ", "wget ", "nc ", " -i", "base64", "python", "/tmp/") or FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash", "/sh", "dash", "zsh", "cmd.exe", "powershell", "pwsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c", "/dev/tcp/", "curl ", "wget ", "nc ", " -i", "base64", "python", "/tmp/") or ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Flowise node.js spawns Unix shell/command binaries as root (CSVAgent Pyodide RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the core of CVE-2026-69255: the Flowise node.js process using Pyodide's js bridge to call process.mainModule.constructor._load('child_process').execSync() and spawn OS commands as root (PID 1 in container). A node process that is a Flowise workflow engine should never fork /bin/sh, id, uname, or whoami — that child is the injected payload executing. Rationale: Grounded in the verified chain (process.mainModule.constructor._load('child_process').execSync('id') as root, PID 1). A node parent forking a shell/recon binary is the direct RCE observable; requiring AccountName=root matches the article's verified 'Server username: root'. Cross-checked GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv / CVE-2026-41264 confirming the same CSVAgent→pyodide→child_process path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-41264/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise/LangChain nodes that legitimately shell out to a Python tool via a custom Tool node (env, python3)
  • Container entrypoint/health-check scripts where node is the init process invoking sh at startup
  • CI/build images where node runs as root and calls git/curl during package install
  • Admin exec-ing into the container and running id/uname for troubleshooting (parent would be sh, not node)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules","npm","yarn","pnpm","/healthz","docker-entrypoint") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a raw `id`/`uname`/`sh -c` with no Flowise tool wrapper, executed as root under a node parent, is a true positive. Confirm the host runs Flowise <=3.1.2. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate/kill the container, rotate FLOWISE_PASSWORD and any API keys under /root/.flowise, and block the source IP hitting /api/v1/prediction. 3) HUNT: On the same host pivot to outbound connections from node/sh (reverse shell UC), reads of /root/.flowise and /etc/passwd, and the upstream POST /api/v1/chatflows + /api/v1/prediction requests that delivered the payload.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","uname","whoami","cat","env","curl","wget","python3")
| where AccountName == "root" or InitiatingProcessAccountName == "root"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/id","/uname","/whoami","/cat","/env","/curl","/wget","/python3")
| where ActorUsername == "root" or TargetUsername == "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reverse shell / Meterpreter egress from Flowise node or its shell child AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the verified Meterpreter reverse_tcp session by flagging outbound public connections initiated by the Flowise node process or a shell it spawned, on ports other than normal web/DNS. Port-agnostic (not tied to the article's 4444) so it survives operator payload changes. Rationale: Article verifies a Meterpreter session opened from the exploited node process (172.17.0.2 -> 172.17.0.1:4444). Pivoting on node/shell as the initiating process to a public IP on a non-web port catches the reverse shell without hardcoding the port. Sentinel left empty: ImNetworkSession carries no process attribution, so the node/shell parent constraint cannot be expressed on available Sentinel tables. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://www.securityweek.com/exploit-code-published-for-critical-flowise-rce-vulnerability/amp/
ATT&CKT1571 T1059.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise node making outbound LLM/vector-DB API calls on non-standard ports (e.g. self-hosted Ollama :11434, Qdrant :6333)
  • node connecting to a database backend (Postgres :5432, MySQL :3306)
  • Monitoring/APM agents launched by node (StatsD/OTLP ports)
  • Package registry pulls over a proxy on a custom port during container build
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs") and RemotePort in (11434, 6333, 5432, 3306, 6379))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Resolve RemoteIP ownership and reputation; a public IP with no PTR/vendor mapping reached from a freshly-spawned sh child of node is high-confidence C2. Check for a preceding node->sh spawn (UC1). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the container, blackhole the RemoteIP at the egress firewall, and capture memory if IR requires the Meterpreter stager. 3) HUNT: Search for the same RemoteIP/ASN across other Flowise hosts and for staged download commands (curl/wget) in node child command lines.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","sh","bash","dash")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemotePort !in (80, 443, 53)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc

DeviceNetworkEvents

| order by FirstSeen desc

System-recon commands executed under Flowise node/shell context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation discovery burst the PoC demonstrates (id, uname -a, cat /etc/hostname) run as children of node or a node-spawned shell. Targets both recon binaries and reads of sensitive host files that reveal container/host identity. Rationale: PoC output shows id, uname -a and cat /etc/hostname run immediately after the shell opens. Requiring a node/shell parent plus >=2 distinct recon actions distinguishes attacker enumeration from a single benign uname. /root/.flowise and /etc/passwd are the exact sensitive targets the article names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv
ATT&CKT1082 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container entrypoint scripts running uname/hostname to set labels
  • Health checks or app code that reads /etc/hostname for self-identification
  • Ops staff running id/whoami after exec-ing into the container
  • Backup/monitoring jobs that grep /etc/passwd for account inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker-entrypoint","healthcheck","/entrypoint.sh") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Look at command ordering and timing — id -> uname -> cat /etc/hostname within seconds under a node-spawned shell is hands-on-keyboard recon, not a startup script. 2) CONTAIN: Snapshot then isolate the container; preserve shell history. 3) HUNT: Follow with credential-store access (UC4) and outbound C2 (UC2) from the same PID/host, and review who triggered the originating /api/v1/prediction call.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","sh","bash","dash")
| where (FileName in~ ("id","uname","whoami","hostname","env"))
     or (FileName in~ ("cat","head","grep") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/hostname","/root/.flowise"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), DistinctCmds=dcount(FileName), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName
| where DistinctCmds >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs","sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/id","/uname","/whoami","/hostname","/env")
     or (ActingProcessName has_any ("/cat","/head","/grep") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/hostname","/root/.flowise"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), DistinctCmds=dcount(ActingProcessName), Cmds=make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 20) by DvcHostname, ParentProcessName, ActorUsername
| where DistinctCmds >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc

Access to Flowise credential store /root/.flowise and secret env vars AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the verified credential theft: reads of the Flowise SQLite/config store at /root/.flowise (DATABASE_PATH) and dumping of FLOWISE_PASSWORD / APIKEY_PATH secrets from a node-spawned shell. These exact strings appear in the article's post-exploitation output. Rationale: The article's 'Additional Verified Impact / Credential Theft' block names FLOWISE_PASSWORD, DATABASE_PATH=/root/.flowise and APIKEY_PATH verbatim. These are high-fidelity literals; a shell child of node referencing them is credential harvesting, not normal Flowise operation (the app reads its own DB via the node process, not via cat/grep). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/migration scripts that tar or copy /root/.flowise
  • Ops staff grepping env for DATABASE_PATH during troubleshooting
  • Container entrypoint exporting FLOWISE_PASSWORD/DATABASE_PATH at startup (parent would be the init shell, not node)
  • Config-management tooling templating the Flowise env file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker-entrypoint","/entrypoint.sh","backup","rsync","tar "))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the accessing process is a shell child of node rather than the entrypoint; a cat/grep of /root/.flowise from an interactive-looking shell is theft. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately rotate FLOWISE_PASSWORD, the SQLite DB credentials and every API key stored under /root/.flowise and APIKEY_PATH; revoke downstream tokens (OpenAI, vector DB). 3) HUNT: Check outbound transfers (UC2) that could have exfiltrated the store, and review auth logs for the leaked admin password being reused elsewhere.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/root/.flowise", "FLOWISE_PASSWORD", "APIKEY_PATH", "DATABASE_PATH")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Flowise CSVAgent exploit HTTP sequence: chatflow create + prediction trigger AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the delivery pattern for CVE-2026-69255 at the web tier: an authenticated client creating a chatflow (POST /api/v1/chatflows) then invoking it (POST /api/v1/prediction/<UUID>) — the two-request pattern every public PoC/Metasploit module uses to plant and fire the CSVAgent payload. Rationale: External corroboration (GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv, GitLab GLAD) confirms exploitation = POST /api/v1/chatflows to create the malicious CSVAgent flow, then POST /api/v1/prediction/<UUID> to execute it. Requiring both endpoints from one source in a window is the article-specific delivery fingerprint. Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty: this is web-proxy telemetry with no clean endpoint-EDR or CloudTrail equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/GHSA-9wc7-mj3f-74xv/ • https://gbhackers.com/six-flowise-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Flowise builders creating and testing chatflows during normal development
  • Automated CI/CD or IaC that programmatically provisions chatflows then smoke-tests them via /prediction
  • Load-testing or synthetic-monitoring hitting the prediction API
  • A single power user rapidly iterating on a flow
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the request bodies (if the proxy captures them) and look for the CSVAgent payload markers `import js`, `child_process`, `_load`, or `execSync` and the comma-free breakout `";import js`; correlate SourceIP with an authenticated session. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP, force-expire the attacker's Flowise session/token, and take the instance off the internet until patched to >=3.1.3. 3) HUNT: On the Flowise host, pivot to node->shell spawns (UC1), credential-store access (UC4) and reverse-shell egress (UC2) originating shortly after the /prediction call.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse-shell egress from Flowise node process tree (nc/shell child dialing out)

Flowise/node process spawning Unix shell or netcat reverse shell (CVE-2026-69254 vm2 escape) AIInstallation High
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the CVE-2026-69254 vm2 sandbox escape: the Flowise 'node' process spawning /bin/sh, bash, nc, ncat or socat with reverse-shell markers. A node-parent-to-shell edge carrying /dev/tcp or nc -e is the highest-fidelity signal of the escape reaching child_process. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact escape endpoint (node child_process launching a reverse shell) and the PoC's nc pattern to 172.17.0.1:1337; node-parent-to-shell with /dev/tcp or nc -e is a rare, high-fidelity edge. Cross-checked vm2-escape-to-child_process behaviour against the vm2 advisory wave and Flowise active-exploitation reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3769-jgqc-cxm7 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/vm2-nodejs-library-vulnerabilities.html • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/flowise_js_rce/
ATT&CKT1211 T1059.004 T1059.007 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based build tooling (node-gyp, prebuild, npm/yarn lifecycle scripts) forking sh -c during image builds
  • Flowise/node worker legitimately shelling out to ffmpeg/imagemagick/git via child_process for document processing
  • Container healthcheck scripts using nc to test port reachability of a downstream service
  • Developer or CI running a node app interactively that spawns bash for a subprocess helper
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","npm ","yarn ","node_modules/.bin","/usr/bin/ffmpeg","convert ","git ")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the node parent's InitiatingProcessCommandLine; confirm the shell/nc invocation carries a reverse-shell shape (/dev/tcp, -e /bin/sh, mkfifo) and identify the remote endpoint. Check whether the host runs Flowise and is internet-reachable. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/container, kill the node and child shell PIDs, and block the observed remote IP:port at the egress firewall. Rotate any secrets (E2B/API keys, DB creds) reachable from the Flowise process. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the node PID for outbound connections (UC2), review Flowise API/auth logs for the preceding AgentAsTool/baseURL config change, and search other Flowise hosts for the same parent-child edge.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("child_process","/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo")
| where FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","npm ","yarn ","node_modules/.bin"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","child_process")
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","node_modules/.bin"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
