Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-04 16 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Nearly half of C2 malware bypasses DNS by connecting directly to IP addresses. Zero trust IP enforcement secures networks against these threats. The post Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phorpiex dropper D2IP payload retrieval from 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SectopRAT in-browser proxy /churl traffic mirroring to attacker IPs · [LLM] Hardcoded WebSocket backdoor to 154.92.19.71:39989 (no DNS) · [LLM] ZT-IP hunt: direct-to-IP egress with no preceding DNS resolution · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Custom \GET obfuscated exfiltration to 18.228.188.56 / SHA256-tracked sample · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phorpiex dropper D2IP payload retrieval from 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts direct-to-IP HTTP GETs to the Phorpiex/Trik staging host 178.16.54.109, which serves loaders (st.exe, 32.exe/64.exe, twizt.exe, xmrig.exe) and staged config paths (/1../6, /sex/k/n.txt, /new.php). Article-specific because the IP is a confirmed long-running Phorpiex delivery node contacted with no preceding DNS query. Rationale: IP 178.16.54.109 is a confirmed Phorpiex C2/loader host (corroborated by Bitsight and executemalware IOC repo serving 32.exe/64.exe/twizt.exe/xmrig.exe), contacted D2IP with no DNS — a high-fidelity, low-FP anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/ransomware-twizt-inside-phorpiex-botnet • https://github.com/executemalware/Malware-IOCs/blob/main/2024-03-28%20Phorpiex%20IOCs • https://otx.alienvault.com/pulse/606aea55d76b8a0aeccfa377
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/sandbox VM detonating samples against the C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IP
  • Honeypot or deception host beaconing to the IP by design
  • Shared-hosting reuse if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant (validate WHOIS/timeframe)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\SandBox\", @"\Analysis\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and its SHA256; pull any file written from the host (st.exe/windrv.exe/sysmgnrsv.exe) via DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block 178.16.54.109 at egress, and quarantine the dropped loader. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256 org-wide, XMRig persistence, and Run-key/service autoruns pointing at %userprofile% driver-look-alike names.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "178.16.54.109"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "178.16.54.109"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SectopRAT in-browser proxy /churl traffic mirroring to attacker IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts SectopRAT (ArechClient2) in-browser proxy beacons to 87.120.107.33 and 194.76.227.94, and the /churl endpoint that relays every visited URL (including authenticated session pages) to the operator. Article-specific because two distinct actors deployed the same family against education using these exact IPs and the /churl proxy path. Rationale: Two named SectopRAT proxy IPs plus the malware-specific /churl relay path give an IP-and-path double anchor; SectopRAT's browser-proxy/BrowserLogging capability is corroborated by Darktrace/G DATA write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/not-your-average-rodent-darktraces-mitigation-of-the-sectop-remote-access-trojan-rat • https://www.gdatasoftware.com/blog/2021/02/36633-new-version-adds-encrypted-communication
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1185 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal API that happens to expose a /churl path (validate against the named IPs)
  • Corporate forward-proxy appliance whose logs mirror URLs (matches /churl only if such a path exists internally)
  • Sandbox detonation of SectopRAT samples by the SOC
  • IP reassignment on shared hosting after the campaign window
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process holding the socket (SectopRAT often injects into or masquerades as a browser/.NET host) and capture its SHA256; review /churl payloads for exfiltrated session URLs. 2) Contain: isolate host, block both IPs, force-reset credentials for any authenticated sessions seen relayed. 3) Hunt: search DeviceProcessEvents for the injecting .NET binary, secondary desktop creation, and other hosts beaconing to either IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94") or RemoteUrl has "/churl"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94") or RequestURL has "/churl"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Custom \GET obfuscated exfiltration to 18.228.188.56 / SHA256-tracked sample AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the persistent \GET (backslash-GET) exfiltration campaign: a malformed HTTP method followed by a 250–666 char structured-encoded blob, beaconing to Brazil-cloud IP 18.228.188.56 with rotating ports. Anchored on the named IP and the disassembled sample hash so it survives the actor's IP/port rotation OpSec. Rationale: Dual anchor: the named C2 IP 18.228.188.56 plus the disassembled sample SHA256 cc43cd… — the hash survives the campaign's documented IP/port rotation, and the \GET method string catches proxy-visible variants. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workload hosted in the same AWS sa-east-1 (Brazil) range if the IP is reassigned post-campaign
  • Proxy that URL-encodes methods and false-matches on a backslash before GET
  • SOC malware detonation of the tracked sample
  • Vulnerability scanner malforming HTTP methods against the host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process matches SHA256 cc43cd… and inspect SentBytes / the encoded blob length (250–666 chars) for exfil volume. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the IP, and preserve the process binary for the encoding-scheme keys noted in the article. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 across all hosts, look for the same 250–666 char \GET pattern to other rotating IPs/ports, and scope impacted sectors (gov/airline/university assets).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "18.228.188.56"
   or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "18.228.188.56" or RequestMethod contains "\\GET"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestMethod, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, SentBytes, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hardcoded WebSocket backdoor to 154.92.19.71:39989 (no DNS) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the backdoor that opens a WebSocket (wss) directly to the Unicode-hardcoded C2 154.92.19.71 on non-standard port 39989 with zero preceding DNS. Article-specific via the exact IP+port pair extracted from the binary via Ghidra. Rationale: Exact IP+port pair (154.92.19.71:39989) reverse-engineered from the binary as a hardcoded Unicode wss:// string; the non-standard high port plus D2IP makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1071 T1571 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app legitimately using port 39989 to an unrelated host (excluded by the exact IP match)
  • SOC sandbox detonation of the backdoor
  • Deception/honeypot beacon to the IP
  • IP reassignment after the campaign window
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process opening the socket and its SHA256/parent; confirm no DNS query preceded the connection. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 154.92.19.71:39989 at egress, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: extract other hardcoded Unicode IP strings from the sample, sweep for the same binary hash and any other high-port D2IP beacons org-wide.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,

          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DestinationIP == "154.92.19.71" and DestinationPort == 39989
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

ZT-IP hunt: direct-to-IP egress with no preceding DNS resolution AICommand & Control Medium
Encodes the article's zero-trust-IP method — surfacing outbound public-IP connections that carry no resolved domain context (raw IP, no preceding DNS), initiated by non-browser processes. This is how Unit 42 surfaced the Phorpiex, \GET and SectopRAT infrastructure; it is a broad hunting sweep for new D2IP C2 beyond the named IOCs. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's ZT-IP thesis (RemoteUrl empty + public IP = no sanctioning DNS response) and prioritises the five named C2 IPs while surfacing new D2IP infrastructure; scoped to non-browser processes and a burst floor to manage the acknowledged high FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1071 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • NTP/time sync and OS telemetry that legitimately dial IPs directly
  • IP-literal CDN/anycast endpoints (some app updaters, game clients)
  • Monitoring/EDR agents beaconing to hardcoded management IPs
  • P2P/collaboration apps (WebRTC, torrent) using direct-IP mesh
  • Software licensing checks that connect by IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","ntoskrnl.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","w3wp.exe") and RemotePort !in (123, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by the KnownBad flag first, then by rare process+IP pairs; pull the initiating binary's SHA256 and signer. 2) Contain: for any KnownC2 or unsigned/rare binary, isolate the host and block the IP. 3) Hunt: baseline the process→IP pairs over 30 days, promote persistent unexplained D2IP beacons to alerting, and cross-check destinations against threat intel.
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe"]);
let KnownC2 = dynamic(["178.16.54.109","18.228.188.56","87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94","154.92.19.71"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isempty(RemoteUrl)                       // no domain context => direct-to-IP (ZT-IP)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (Browsers)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName)
          by RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| extend KnownBad = RemoteIP in (KnownC2)
| where KnownBad or Conns > 20                   // 20 = burst floor to cut one-off IP checks
| order by KnownBad desc, FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).

DeviceNetworkEvents

| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName)
          by RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 -@DestinationHostname:* -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\iexplore.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or SHA1 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or MD5 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or SHA1 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or MD5 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
Critical

How legitimate cloud platforms enable phishers to bypass MFA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-08-04 9 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

We cover a cloud-based AitM attack scenario leveraging service workers and Ultraviolet, and provide detailed phishing hosting statistics across platforms like Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, and IPFS.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] First-seen browser egress to abused cloud-PaaS phishing domains (workers.dev / pages.dev / vercel.app / github.io / netlify.app / dweb.link) · [LLM] Safe Links click resolving through a cloud-PaaS redirect chain into AitM phishing · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AitM session hijack: PaaS phishing-page visit followed by successful Entra sign-in from a different IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
First-seen browser egress to abused cloud-PaaS phishing domains (workers.dev / pages.dev / vercel.app / github.io / netlify.app / dweb.link) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a corporate browser making its first-ever connection (org-wide baseline anti-join) to a subdomain of the exact free-tier PaaS platforms this campaign abuses to host its AitM CAPTCHA relay and Ultraviolet reverse-proxy pages. Because the parent domains host millions of legit projects, the fidelity comes from the never-before-seen-in-org pivot, not the suffix alone. Rationale: Uses the exact PaaS suffix set from the article's statistics table (pages.dev 24.9%, vercel.app 13.8%, github.io 13.7%, netlify.app 10.0%, dweb.link 7.8%, plus workers.dev from the case study). Baseline anti-join is the noise reducer since these apex domains are shared with legit content. Cross-checked urlscan.io (Ultraviolet campaign) and RingSafe/Cofense Cloudflare-abuse reports. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://urlscan.io/blog/2026/04/15/ProxyingTrust/ • https://ringsafe.in/cloudflare-fronted-phishing-in-2026-how-workers-pages-tunnels-and-r2-became-default-phishing-infrastructure/ • https://cofense.com/blog/how-cloudflare-services-are-abused-for-credential-theft-and-malware-distribution

Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("devops-svc","builder")) and Devices == 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RemoteUrl/DstHostname and fetch it in a sandbox — a genuine hit shows a fake CAPTCHA gate or a Microsoft login iframe/BitB pop-up with a spoofed address bar. Check whether the same user received an inbound email whose link redirected here. 2) Contain: block the specific FQDN at proxy/DNS (not the apex), reset the user's Entra credentials and revoke all sessions/refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: search that user's SigninLogs for a successful MFA-satisfied sign-in from a datacenter/hosting IP within 30 min (AitM token replay) and check for new inbox rules or OAuth grants.

Safe Links click resolving through a cloud-PaaS redirect chain into AitM phishing AIDelivery Medium
Hunts UrlClickEvents where the resolved redirect chain (UrlChain) or final URL lands on one of the campaign's abused PaaS platforms — mirroring the article's Stage 1→2 flow of compromised-site CAPTCHA relay bouncing the victim to a *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy page. Targets the redirect landing, not the innocuous-looking link in the email body. Rationale: Anchors on the article's multi-stage redirect (email link -> compromised site CAPTCHA -> *.workers.dev), so it inspects the Safe Links UrlChain rather than the benign first-hop domain. ClickedThrough is the high-fidelity user-bypass signal. PaaS suffixes taken directly from the article's platform table. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://urlscan.io/blog/2026/04/15/ProxyingTrust/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1583.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit newsletter/marketing tracking link that happens to redirect through a Vercel/Netlify edge function
  • Internal app or CI notification linking to a github.io or pages.dev docs page
  • A vendor's URL-shortener whose final hop is a serverless health page
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platforms hosting lures on PaaS
  • Web3 wallet flows resolving through a dweb.link IPFS gateway
Suppression filter
| where IsClickedThrough == true or Workload == "Email"
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the full UrlChain terminal URL; confirm a Microsoft login iframe/BitB window and check whether the redirect emerged from a compromised legitimate first-hop domain. Confirm ActionType/IsClickedThrough (user actually reached the page). 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete the source message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents ZAP, block the terminal FQDN, force credential reset + session revocation for the clicker. 3) Hunt: enumerate other recipients of the same NetworkMessageId/sender, and pivot each clicker into UC-3 to catch AitM session replay.

AitM session hijack: PaaS phishing-page visit followed by successful Entra sign-in from a different IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates an endpoint browser connecting to a campaign PaaS domain (Stage 2/3 Ultraviolet proxy + BitB) with a successful, MFA-satisfied Entra sign-in for the same user within 30 minutes whose source IP does NOT match the victim's device — the hallmark of the attacker replaying the intercepted session token from their own infrastructure. This is the payoff step the article describes: credentials and MFA relayed, then the attacker holds a live session. Rationale: Expresses the article's core AitM outcome: MFA relayed through the *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy, then the attacker uses the token from their own IP. The IP-mismatch clause (sign-in source != victim device public IP) within a 30-min window of the PaaS visit is the discriminator corroborated by Cofense/Securelist noting the token is replayed from a different IP/ASN than where the victim authenticated. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://cofense.com/blog/how-cloudflare-services-are-abused-for-credential-theft-and-malware-distribution • https://ringsafe.in/cloudflare-fronted-phishing-in-2026-how-workers-pages-tunnels-and-r2-became-default-phishing-infrastructure/
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1111 T1550.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User visits a legit PaaS-hosted app then signs in to M365 over corporate VPN/egress with a different public IP than the device reports
  • Roaming/mobile user whose device PublicIP and sign-in IP legitimately differ (cellular vs Wi-Fi)
  • CDN/proxy egress that rewrites the outbound IP for O365 traffic
  • Shared-device/kiosk scenarios where DeviceInfo PublicIP is stale
  • Developer testing their own Cloudflare Worker while authenticated to Azure
Suppression filter
| where SignInIP !in (dynamic([])) and Country != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sign-in IP is a hosting/datacenter ASN (not corporate egress or the user's ISP) and that the PaaS URL detonates to a Microsoft login/BitB page — that combination is a confirmed token theft. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens/sessions for the account (Entra 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-registration of MFA; block the SignInIP and PaaS FQDN. 3) Hunt: review AuditLogs/CloudAppEvents for attacker-created inbox forwarding rules, new OAuth app consents, MFA method additions, and mailbox exfiltration under that account after the sign-in time.
let Window = 30m;
let PhishConns = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
    | where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".pages.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".vercel.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".github.io" or RemoteUrl endswith ".netlify.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
    | project ConnTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, PhishUrl=RemoteUrl, UserUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn;
let DevIP = DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, PublicIP) by DeviceName;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SignInTime=Timestamp, AccountUpn, SignInIP=IPAddress, Application, Country, City
| join kind=inner PhishConns on $left.AccountUpn == $right.UserUpn
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| join kind=leftouter DevIP on DeviceName
| where isempty(PublicIP) or SignInIP != PublicIP
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), AccountUpn, DeviceName, PhishUrl, SignInIP, DevicePublicIP=PublicIP, Application, Country, City
| order by SignInTime desc
let Window = 30m;
let Phish = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstHostname endswith ".workers.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".pages.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".vercel.app" or DstHostname endswith ".github.io" or DstHostname endswith ".netlify.app" or DstHostname endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(SrcUsername)
    | project ConnTime=TimeGenerated, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, PhishHost=DstHostname;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| project SignInTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP=IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Location
| join kind=inner Phish on $left.UserPrincipalName == $right.SrcUsername
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| where SignInIP != SrcIpAddr
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), UserPrincipalName, PhishHost, SignInIP, VictimIP=SrcIpAddr, AppDisplayName, Location
| order by SignInTime desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Google Deletes 3 ADK AI Workflows After Malicious GitHub Issue Could Trigger Privileged Agent

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 7 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Google deleted three AI agent workflows from its Agent Development Kit (ADK) Python repository. Pillar Security showed that a public GitHub issue could manipulate a triage agent into triggering a privileged code-fixing agent. The researchers said the public agent could be prompt-injected into posting /adk-issue-fix as adk-bot. They identified the bot as a collaborator, so that comment satisfied

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1566 T1566.002

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Git spawning shell/interpreter from runner temp dir (hook payload execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Git core.hooksPath redirected to writable temp dir on CI runner (ADK allowlist bypass)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Git core.hooksPath redirected to writable temp dir on CI runner (ADK allowlist bypass) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the exact code-execution primitive Pillar Security demonstrated against Google's ADK issue-fix workflow: the command allowlist only permitted commands whose first token was gh or git, so the agent wrote a payload and abused `git -c core.hooksPath=<dir>` / `git config core.hooksPath` to make an allowed Git invocation execute attacker-controlled code via a custom hook path. Fires when git is run with core.hooksPath pointing at a runner-writable location. Rationale: Anchors on the exact bypass the article/Pillar describe verbatim ('core.hooksPath can redirect Git to another directory', 'make an allowed Git command execute it through a custom hook path') combined with GitHub-Actions runner-writable paths (/home/runner, /runner/_work, _actions) so it fires on the CI-runner exploitation, not on dev laptops. The .husky exclusion strips the one common legitimate core.hooksPath user. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-deletes-3-adk-ai-workflows-after.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4204906/google-adk-flaws-reveal-what-happens-when-ai-agents-trust-the-wrong-message.html • https://www.scworld.com/news/researchers-find-agent-to-agent-privilege-escalation-in-googles-adk-for-python-repo • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/08/03/google-dev-kit-spurs-first-ever-agent-on-agent-violence/5282496
ATT&CKT1574 T1059.004 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Husky/pre-commit dev tooling setting core.hooksPath to a repo-relative .husky directory (excluded by filter)
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately installs a shared hooks directory under the workspace via git config core.hooksPath
  • Developer running git with an explicit --config core.hooksPath while debugging hooks locally on a self-hosted runner
  • Monorepo bootstrap scripts that point core.hooksPath at a vendored tools directory under _work
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has ".husky" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"core\.hooksPath=(\.|\./|/[^ ]*/repo)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full git command line and the initiating process — confirm the core.hooksPath value points at a writable/temp path and inspect the referenced hooks directory for a freshly-written executable (pre-commit/post-checkout/post-commit). Correlate the runner, workflow run, and triggering issue/PR number. 2) Contain: pause the self-hosted runner and revoke/rotate any PAT, GOOGLE_API_KEY, and GCP service-account key exposed to that job; invalidate the runner's registration token. 3) Hunt: on the same host/AID look for outbound connections from git/curl/python to non-github.com/non-googleapis.com hosts (token exfil), and review recent bot-authored PRs/branches for injected code.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "git"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work","_actions")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has ".husky"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "git" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "git "
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work","_actions")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has ".husky"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Git core.hooksPath Redirected to Writable Runner Directory (ADK CI Abuse)
id: 8f2e1c4a-6b3d-4a1e-9c7f-2d5b8e0a1f34
description: Detects git invoked with core.hooksPath pointing at a runner-writable temp directory, the allowlist-bypass code-execution technique in the Pillar Security ADK issue-fix workflow report.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-deletes-3-adk-ai-workflows-after.html
  - https://www.pillar.security/blog/my-agentic-trust-issues-from-prompt-injection-to-supply-chain-compromise-on-gemini-cli
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1574
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '/git'
  selection_hooks:
    CommandLine|contains: 'core.hooksPath'
  selection_paths:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/var/tmp/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - '/home/runner/'
      - '/runner/_work'
      - '_actions'
  filter_husky:
    CommandLine|contains: '.husky'
  condition: selection_img and selection_hooks and selection_paths and not filter_husky
level: medium
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog OR linux.sysmon) @process.name:git @process.command_line:*core.hooksPath* (@process.command_line:*/tmp/* OR @process.command_line:*/var/tmp/* OR @process.command_line:*/dev/shm/* OR @process.command_line:*/home/runner/* OR @process.command_line:*/runner/_work*) -@process.command_line:*.husky*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/git$/i
| CommandLine=/core\.hooksPath/i
| CommandLine=/(\/tmp\/|\/var\/tmp\/|\/dev\/shm\/|\/home\/runner\/|\/runner\/_work|_actions)/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/\.husky/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=git Processes.process="*core.hooksPath*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Git spawning shell/interpreter from runner temp dir (hook payload execution) AIExploitation Medium
Complements the cmdline hunt by catching the payload actually running: once core.hooksPath is redirected, an 'allowed' git command executes the attacker's hook, so git becomes the parent of a shell/interpreter/downloader launched from a runner-writable path. On a CI runner git rarely spawns bash/python/curl, making the parent=git → interpreter-from-temp pairing high-signal. Rationale: Targets a different pivot than UC1 — the parent/child image relationship rather than a cmdline arg — catching the moment the redirected hook payload runs ('write a payload and make an allowed Git command execute it'). git parenting an interpreter from /runner/_work or /tmp on a self-hosted runner is inherently abnormal, giving high fidelity even without the core.hooksPath string in view. Datadog left empty: the listed linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field, so the parent=git → child pairing cannot be expressed there. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-deletes-3-adk-ai-workflows-after.html • https://www.pillar.security/blog/my-agentic-trust-issues-from-prompt-injection-to-supply-chain-compromise-on-gemini-cli • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/08/03/google-dev-kit-spurs-first-ever-agent-on-agent-violence/5282496
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate git hooks (pre-commit/post-checkout) implemented as shell/python scripts running during a normal CI checkout
  • Husky-managed hooks invoking node from the repo tree
  • Build tooling where git-lfs or a credential helper shells out to a helper script under the workspace
  • Repo bootstrap that runs a setup shell script via a post-merge hook on the runner
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has ".husky" or FolderPath has "/hooks/" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "core.hooksPath")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and script path — determine whether the interpreter is executing a file inside a hooks directory or an unexpected temp path, and whether the git parent used a redirected core.hooksPath (join to UC1 on the same host/time). Identify the workflow run and triggering PR/issue. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, kill the process tree, and rotate every credential the job held (bot PAT, GOOGLE_API_KEY, GCP SA key). 3) Hunt: review outbound traffic from the child process for credential exfiltration to non-GitHub/Google hosts, and check for bot-created forks/branches or PRs opened around the same timestamp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "git"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","node","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/runner/_work"))
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "git"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","node","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work"))
    or (ParentProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Git Spawns Shell or Downloader From Runner Temp Path (Hook Payload Execution)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
