KNUCKLEBALL loader, JAR payload drops & init.d persistence on SonicWall SMA AIInstallation High
Hunts the KNUCKLEBALL Python loader (deploy_new.py in the python3.11 site-packages dir), its two staged JARs (agent_wp8.jar=Suo5, agent_wp9.jar=ORANGETAIL), the xzfind ROOTRUN privesc binary, and the /etc/init.d/workplace persistence edit on compromised SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances. Entirely article/Volexity-specific file artifacts. Rationale: Uses Volexity's exact malware paths (deploy_new.py in site-packages, /tmp/agent_wp8.jar & agent_wp9.jar, /usr/bin/xzfind ROOTRUN, /tmp/1234.sh) plus the 'running hotfix removal for:../' path-traversal log string. SHA256s (8c470301..., ea9154e3..., 1e1e68bb..., 81a9af38...) match these files. Falcon/Defender empty: the appliance is not an EDR-managed host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://socradar.io/blog/sonicwall-sma-knuckleball-malware/
ATT&CKT1037.004 T1059.006 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall firmware/hotfix updates writing to site-packages or modifying /etc/init.d/workplace
  • Vendor support scripts staged under /tmp during a diagnostics session
  • Admin-authored maintenance scripts named similarly in /tmp
  • Backup/AV agents reading (not writing) these paths
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash any deploy_new.py / xzfind / *.jar present and compare to the Volexity SHA256s (deploy_new.py=8c470301..., xzfind=81a9af38..., agent_wp9.jar/ORANGETAIL=ea9154e3..., agent_wp8.jar/Suo5=1e1e68bb...). 2) Contain: power-isolate and rebuild the appliance from clean firmware - JVM-injected payloads survive simple file deletion; remove the deploy_new.py line from /etc/init.d/workplace. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC4 (tcpdump LDAP capture), review /var/lib/unit/conf.json for the 8085 proxy route, and rotate credentials/TOTP seeds harvested from the appliance.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("deploy_new.py","/tmp/agent_wp8.jar","/tmp/agent_wp9.jar","/usr/bin/xzfind","/tmp/1234.sh","running hotfix removal for:../")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

tcpdump LDAP credential sniffing on SonicWall SMA appliance AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the UTA0533 credential-harvesting step where tcpdump is run on a compromised SonicWall SMA appliance to capture cleartext LDAP (TCP 389) authentication traffic, driven by the /var/tmp/lib.sh helper. Article/Volexity-specific credential-access behaviour on the appliance itself. Rationale: Uses Volexity's documented credential-harvesting command (tcpdump on TCP 389 for cleartext LDAP) and the /var/tmp/lib.sh storage helper. Medium confidence/FP because admins do legitimately run tcpdump - the LDAP-389 + /var/tmp/lib.sh combination is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.securityweek.com/sonicwall-zero-days-exploited-to-deliver-custom-malware-for-weeks-before-patch/
ATT&CKT1040 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Appliance admin running tcpdump for legitimate LDAP/AD connectivity troubleshooting
  • SonicWall vendor support capturing a diagnostic packet trace
  • Monitoring/observability agents performing periodic packet captures
  • Scheduled config-backup scripts unrelated to lib.sh
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/session that launched tcpdump and whether a capture file was written under /var/tmp; correlate the timestamp to any UC1/UC2 exploitation hit. 2) Contain: kill the tcpdump process, isolate the appliance, and treat all LDAP/AD credentials that authenticated through it as compromised. 3) Hunt: rotate the exposed directory-service credentials and TOTP MFA seeds immediately, then hunt for use of those creds via internal auth logs and for Suo5-tunneled lateral movement.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (SyslogMessage has "tcpdump" and (SyslogMessage has " 389" or SyslogMessage has "port 389" or SyslogMessage has "ldap")) or SyslogMessage has "/var/tmp/lib.sh"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

INC Ransomware encryption: .inc mass file writes and INC-README notes AIActions on Objectives High
Detects INC Ransomware's on-host impact stage on internal Windows endpoints reached via the SonicWall SMA foothold: high-volume file writes/renames to the .inc extension plus creation of INC-README.txt / INC-README.html ransom notes. Enriched from SentinelOne/Huntress INC artifacts since the article names the actor but not the note/extension. Rationale: Article names INC Ransomware as the dominant actor; SentinelOne and Huntress confirm INC writes INC-README.txt/.html notes and appends the .inc extension. The 5-minute >100-file threshold OR any ransom-note write is the mass-encryption discriminator and separates it from benign .inc include files. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/inc-ransom/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/investigating-new-inc-ransom-group-activity • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer machines mass-writing .inc PHP/ASP/CAD include files during a build (excluded by dev-tool filter + threshold)
  • Backup or archival software touching many files with an .inc-suffixed temp name
  • Legacy applications that legitimately use .inc as a data extension
  • Bulk file-server migration jobs generating high write counts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msbuild.exe","devenv.exe","php.exe","cmake.exe","node.exe") or Notes > 0
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged DeviceName confirm the InitiatingProcess writing .inc files is not a known dev/build tool and that INC-README.txt/.html notes exist; check InitiatingProcessSHA256 against INC IOCs. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network immediately, suspend the offending process, and disable the associated account; snapshot for forensics before any reboot. 3) Hunt: trace the intrusion back to the SMA 1000 (UC1-UC4), check for VSS deletion/backup tampering, and sweep all hosts reachable via the compromised VPN for the same .inc/INC-README pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".inc" or FileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")
| summarize FileCount = count(), Notes = countif(FileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), Folders = dcount(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 100 or Notes > 0
| sort by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "inc" or TargetFileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")
| summarize FileCount = count(), Notes = countif(TargetFileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 5) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 100 or Notes > 0
| sort by FileCount desc

UTA0533/INC SonicWall exploitation source-IP network IOCs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoint or network communication with the four Volexity-confirmed UTA0533 exploitation/web-shell source IPs (108.205.8.173, 147.45.51.19, 150.241.210.53, 81.19.140.217) used against SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances. Surfaces both inbound appliance interaction and any Suo5-tunneled traffic seen by internal hosts. Rationale: Uses only the four non-VPN sample IPs Volexity published (the campaign also used 200+ ExpressVPN/Mullvad exits, which would be too noisy to ship). Dropped helprans.com and four other article-only IPs (202.8.105.201, 217.77.15.99, 42.200.172.14, 89.117.20.1) as single-source per corroboration rules. Medium confidence because IPs can be reassigned. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195626/hacking/volexity-uncovers-zero-day-campaign-targeting-sonicwall-vpn-appliances.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign users behind a recycled datacenter/VPN IP that was previously attacker-controlled
  • Threat-intel or ASM scanning services legitimately probing your perimeter from a listed IP
  • IP reassigned by the hosting provider to a new tenant after the campaign
  • Internal proxy egressing many users' traffic through one of these addresses
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine direction - inbound to the SMA 1000 (exploitation source) vs an internal host reaching out (possible tunneled C2); pull the process (InitiatingProcessFileName) on any internal hit. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at the perimeter and, for any internal host that contacted them, isolate and inspect for web-shell/Suo5 activity. 3) Hunt: correlate the IP timestamps with UC1/UC2 web-log hits, verify appliance patch level, and rotate credentials/TOTP seeds if the appliance interacted with these IPs.

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-15409", "CVE-2026-15410")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

            - '\lsm.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

        | where SHA256 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or SHA1 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or MD5 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or SHA1 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or MD5 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Potato privilege-escalation tooling (GodPotato / SweetPotato / BadPotato) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — An analysis of incidents at Brazilian educational institutions
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-access batch script observed in the leaked-LockBit-builder case that enabled RDP by setting fDenyTSConnections to 0 and disabled endpoint defenses before ransomware deployment. Anchors on the exact registry value/data pair the article's script wrote. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim registry write from the article's disable-defenses batch script (HKLM\...\Control\Terminal Server \ fDenyTSConnections = 0) which turns RDP on; pairs it with reg.exe execution to keep fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-builder-leaked-online-by-angry-developer/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately enabling RDP on a new server build via a provisioning script
  • GPO/DSC/Intune configuration baseline that manages fDenyTSConnections
  • MSP onboarding automation that turns on RDP for remote management
  • Server 2016 role-setup wizards that toggle Remote Desktop
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","omadmclient.exe","gpscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating account and parent process of the reg.exe/registry write; confirm whether the same host also saw EDR/Defender service stops in the surrounding minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the account used to write the value, and re-set fDenyTSConnections to 1 if the change was unauthorized. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP (LogonType 10) and search for PsExecSvc.exe/named ransomware payloads (1.exe, LBB.exe) and Defender-tamper events fleet-wide.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Terminal Server"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "fDenyTSConnections"
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SystemSettings.exe","ServerManager.exe","mmc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| where CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections" and CommandLine has_any ("/d 0","/d 0x0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the manual lateral deployment of the custom LockBit build from the leaked builder: the sample was configured without psexec_netspread, so operators used PsExec (PsExecSvc.exe) to remotely launch ransomware binaries named 1.EXE and LBB.exe. Targets the impact/deployment step, not generic PsExec admin use. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim payload names (1.EXE, LBB.exe) and the PsExecSvc.exe service the operators relied on for manual spread after building a variant without psexec_netspread; combining parent + payload names keeps the otherwise-generic 1.exe fidelity acceptable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1486 T1569.002 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin using Sysinternals PsExec for remote software rollout (PsExecSvc.exe as parent)
  • Automation/RMM that names a tool 1.exe in a temp build path
  • Software packaging test binaries transiently named 1.exe
  • Remote patch scripts pushed via PsExec across a fleet
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\SCCM\\","\\ccmcache\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 and full path of the spawned binary and the source host driving PsExecSvc.exe; check for mass DeviceFileEvents FileRenamed/FileModified bursts on the same device. 2) Contain: network-isolate affected hosts, block the payload hash, and disable the deploying account. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where PsExecSvc.exe appeared (USN Journal .KEY artifacts corroborate historic spread), look for kill_defender/Defender-uninstall events and wallpaper/registry changes indicative of LockBit encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "PsExecSvc.exe"
    or FileName in~ ("1.exe","LBB.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\PsExecSvc.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\1.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\LBB.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potato privilege-escalation tooling (GodPotato / SweetPotato / BadPotato) AIExploitation High
Hunts the SeImpersonate token-abuse tools the article attributes to the observed privilege-escalation activity in these intrusions. Anchors on the exact tool family names used to move from a service/valid account to SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the three Potato variant names the article explicitly attributes to privilege escalation (GodPotato, SweetPotato, BadPotato); these are offensive-only tool names, so name/cmdline matches are high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/
ATT&CKT1134.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / pentest engagement running Potato tools with authorization
  • Security researcher detonating the tools in a sandbox VM
  • A file legitimately containing the substring 'potato' in an unrelated business name (rare, mitigated by path/cmdline context)
  • Malware-analysis training lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Tools\RedTeam\", @"\PurpleTeam\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating (pre-escalation) account and whether the resulting process/child ran at SYSTEM integrity; review parent process (often a service or web-app pool identity). 2) Contain: isolate the host and reset credentials for the abused service/valid account. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for follow-on SYSTEM-level actions — Defender-disable batch scripts, RDP enablement (fDenyTSConnections=0), PsExec spread, and ransomware payload drops.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
    or CommandLine has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the attacker-driven AnyDesk deployment the article ties to DragonForce (Case 02): AnyDesk installed and configured for unattended access to give operators remote control before ransomware. Anchors on the unattended-install command-line flags rather than mere presence of AnyDesk. Rationale: Anchors on AnyDesk (named in Case 02 as the DragonForce remote-access vector) combined with unattended-install flags that legitimate interactive users rarely pass, corroborated by DragonForce write-ups documenting silent AnyDesk installs for persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/dragonforce-ransomware-attack/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1219 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk legitimately deploying AnyDesk unattended via GPO/RMM
  • MSP standardizing on AnyDesk for remote support with --start-with-win
  • User self-installing AnyDesk from a legit MSI that passes --silent
  • Vendor support session where AnyDesk is provisioned with a set password
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the installing account and parent process (deployment tool vs. email client vs. script) and whether AnyDesk is a sanctioned tool for this host/OU. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill AnyDesk, and rotate credentials; capture the AnyDesk ID/anydesk.trace for the incoming operator IP. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents for AnyDesk relay traffic (boot.net.anydesk.com / *.relay), then look for DragonForce indicators — PsExec spread, mass encryption, ransom notes — across hosts that ran AnyDesk in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AnyDesk.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password","--get-id")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    object payload signature.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

status: experimental
description: |

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
